look_here_first: FIRST measure the green involucre UNDER the flower heads (excluding florets and projecting phyllary spines): local Texas thistle specimen descriptions give roughly 15–20 mm in height. SECOND examine a stem LEAF NODE: the broad sessile upper leaf may make small spine-tipped clasping ears (auricles) and CAN continue as DECURRENT, SPINY STEM WINGS on robust plants. Do not assume wings mean introduced C. vulgare! Instead compare bull thistle's short bristle-spines emerging on the UPPER leaf blade. Check whitish glutinous longitudinal phyllary midridges where visible. C. horridulum has markedly larger 40–45 mm involucres in Williamson County specimens, largely hidden by a separate ring of spinescent upper leaves.

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Erect thistle, usually under about 1 m.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Middle/upper sessile leaves may have broad clasping auricles AND may extend as spiny decurrent wings. Image confirmation requires attachment on the same stem. The upper leaf surface is thinly cobwebby/tomentose, lower face densely white-woolly; C. vulgare has diagnostic stiff short spines on the upper blade.

key_traits.label: Heads
key_traits.text: Purple to pink discoid heads, solitary or in small groups; no ray florets.

key_traits.label: Phyllaries
key_traits.text: Involucre around 12–20 mm high (FNA key and UT Austin detailed Texas treatment). Outer/middle phyllaries often carry a narrow whitish, sticky, glutinous medial ridge; UT Austin describes ~2.5–4 mm ridge on sampled phyllaries. A visible pale line need not be sticky in every photo and is not exclusive among Cirsium.

key_traits.label: Best field traits
key_traits.text: native Texas roadside thistle; pink-purple discoid heads; spiny but not extremely woolly foliage; relatively compact stature

key_traits.label: Stem
key_traits.text: UT Austin Williamson flora documents ridged, somewhat winged stems on robust Texas thistle, with about two spinescent decurrent wings from each cauline leaf. This OVERLAPS winged C. vulgare; do not use a winged/not-winged rule.

lookalikes.differences: C. horridulum has the extra under-head collar of very spinescent upper leaves and a much larger involucre (~40–45 mm in UT Williamson description) compared with C. texanum's ~15–20 mm. C. texanum upper stem leaf bases can clasp with auricles OR descend as spiny wings on robust plants; C. vulgare also has wings but distinctive short bristle-spines on upper LEAF FACE. Do not teach winged/not-winged as an absolute species split.
